title: From Tadpole to Frog
objective: After this level you can explain how a tadpole turns into a frog.
summary: A tadpole has gills, a finned tail and no legs. Hind legs come first, then lungs and front legs; the tail is absorbed. Gudernatsch (1912) showed thyroid hormone drives it.

cards.headline: A tadpole never drops its tail. Its body absorbs it.
cards.body: Somewhere between two months and three years, a swimming larva with gills rebuilds itself into a frog with lungs and legs. Here's the order of the work, and the chemical that gives the orders.

cards.headline: Barely a frog at all
cards.body: A young tadpole looks nothing like its parents. It usually has gills, a long, finned tail and no limbs at all, and it's often a plant-eater. Everything about it is built for life underwater: it breathes with gills where its parents will use lungs. To become a frog, almost every part has to be rebuilt.

events.label: Lungs develop and the front legs appear
The tail shrinks as the body absorbs it, and the mouth turns froglike
The gills disappear, just before it becomes a frog

cards.fact: In 1912, tadpoles fed horse thyroid changed early.
cards.context: Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles bits of several horse organs. Only the thyroid gland sped up their metamorphosis. Later, removing a tadpole's own thyroid stopped the change entirely: without thyroid hormone, the rebuild never happens. Level 10's gray tree frog, algae-eater as a tadpole and insect-hunter as an adult, goes through this same hormone-driven makeover.

cards.headline: Metamorphosis: explained
learned: Tadpoles: gills, finned tail, no legs, often plant-eaters
Hind legs first, then lungs and front legs
The tail is absorbed; the gills vanish last
Without thyroid hormone, there's no frog

questions.prompt: In a growing tadpole, which legs appear first?

options.label: The front legs
options.rationale: The front legs come later, with the lungs.

options.label: All four at once
options.rationale: The hind legs lead the way.

options.label: None until it leaves the water
options.rationale: The legs grow while it's still a tadpole.

questions.explanation: Metamorphosis begins as the hind legs sprout; the front legs appear later, around when the lungs develop.

questions.prompt: What did Gudernatsch's 1912 feeding experiment reveal about metamorphosis?

options.label: Tadpoles need meat to grow legs
options.rationale: He tested organs, and only the thyroid mattered.

options.label: Something from the thyroid gland triggers it
Any horse organ speeds it up
options.rationale: Only the thyroid sped it up.

options.label: It depends only on water temperature
options.rationale: The experiment pointed to the thyroid, a hormone gland.

questions.explanation: Only thyroid tissue sped up metamorphosis, and removing a tadpole's thyroid stops it: thyroid hormone drives the change.

questions.prompt: Level 10's gray tree frog eats algae as a tadpole and insects as an adult. How does metamorphosis explain the switch?

options.label: Adult frogs forget how to digest plants
options.rationale: It's a full rebuild of the body, not forgetting.

options.label: The tadpole's body is rebuilt for hunting
Algae stop growing once the tadpole is older
options.rationale: The change is in the frog, not the algae.

options.label: Insects live only on land, far from ponds
options.rationale: The diet change comes from the new body, not from where insects live.

questions.explanation: Metamorphosis rebuilds a gilled, often plant-eating tadpole into a frog with a froglike mouth, and the gray tree frog's diet shifts to insects with it.
